newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia's oldest hill station faces development.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia's oldest hill station faces development.

text.p: When George Maxwell visited his bungalow at the top of the 1,250-metre (4,100 feet) hill in Malaysia named after him, he was carried by grunting coolies in a sedan chair.
That was more than a century ago. And things haven't changed much since Maxwell was the British colonial administrator in Malaysia's northern state of Perak.
The two ramshackle guest houses were built in 1880 and look like it. Rooms cost a mere 15 ringgit ($6) a night.

Several old bungalows, which tourists can also rent, are scattered about the peak where once a thriving tea estate operated. About 50 people at the most can stay at this state-run hill station at any one time.

A narrow, paved road, winding 13 kilometres (eight miles) up the hill and featuring 72 hairpin turns, was finally built in 1948 with "help" from Japanese prisoners of war. But only state-owned Land Rovers can ferry the few visitors up the hill.
Now Malaysia's oldest and sleepiest hill resort is about to get ready for some 21st century spiff under a plan that has environmentalists and some local residents up in arms.

A company owned by the Malay teachers cooperative and linked to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation plans to spend 75 million ringgit ($30 million) to develop the hill station.

A cable-car would cut across those hairpin turns and haul an expected surge of visitors to the peak. The plans also include a hotel, suspension bridge, lookout tower, seminar centre and botanical gardens.
The company, Guru-Guru Melayu Malaysia Barat Holdings Sdn Bhd, would be given a 10-year concession before handing the project back to the state government.

In return, the company would be given a 12-hectare (30 acres) piece of land at the Taiping Lake Gardens at the foot of the hill to build a shopping complex, resort hotel, medical centre and apartments, among other things.
Mohamed Noor, a Land Rover driver with the state government, said he's all for the development. "Then more people will come. It will be good for business."
In the next breath he adds that trees would be felled and the road widened to accommodate more traffic.

"There will be less cooling air. It will be more like Cameron Highlands," Mohamed said, referring to Malaysia's most well-known hill resort which has seen rampant commercialisation in recent years. "Good for business."
The prospect that Maxwell Hill could be turned into another Cameron Highlands sends chills up and down the spines of local environmentalists.

"It looks like the scale of it could be a problem," said Francis Cheang of the Malaysian Nature Society. "It's a relatively small resort and it would have too big an impact with such a large scale development."

The Malaysian Nature Society and a coalition of other environmental groups have launched a campaign against a federal government plan to build a 2.5 billion ringgit ($1 billion) highway along the main range that bisects the peninsula.

The highway would link three of Malaysia's main hill resorts -- the casino haven in Genting Highlands, the old tea plantations of Cameron Highlands and Fraser Hill, named after a misanthropic turn-of-the-century tin miner.
The coalition argues the highway is unnecessary, would cause severe erosion that would pollute the water supply and promote commercial development along the road, further damaging the environment.
The government says it is spending 3.5 million ringgit on an Environmental Impact Assessment for the project which would take into account suggestions from the environmental groups.
Maxwell Hill, which would not be part of the highway project, remains one of the prettiest spots in Malaysia -- and the wettest, as well, with annual rainfall of 198 inches (502 cms).

When the rains halt and the mist that usually enshrouds the peak lifts, the view is one of the finest in the country. Majestic hornbills cruise the treetops and butterflies with nearly foot-long wing spans flit among the wildflowers.

At the foot of the peak is the Taiping Lake Gardens. Beyond the gardens, the northern Perak plain rolls out, scarred with the open-face tin mines that drew British prospectors and colonial administrators in their wake a century ago.
And on a clear day, one can see the Malacca Strait and Pangkor island shimmering in the distance.
($1=2.5 ringgit)
